reviews.text: 如今同类叙事的作品太多，遭受时间洗礼后，这套美利坚价值观不免有些令人乏味。文戏和战争戏的比重基本持平，战场所带来的震撼感凸显了电影工业的重量，对声景的使用，米勒的两次耳鸣和画面抽帧，将极度刺激的氛围做出了层次感。公路片的架构，寻找瑞恩的旅程也见证了血腥的屠杀，每个人都以国家的名义释放隐藏的恶，无意义的战争，又因为寻找瑞恩而多了些有意义的部分。刚好影片上映的年代，参加过二战的士兵都步入了古稀之年，八人救一人的选择，林肯的名义，美国国旗的落点，都在把大国与小家的关系进行调和，不过讲小家始终是为了歌颂大国，生命如草芥的情况下家族也不能被绝代，是十分商业的对人道主义的呼吁。

Ça me fait penser au dilemme du tramway mais c’est comme si ils avaient rien compris. J’ai eu l’impression de voir une propagande bizarre et c’était telleeeeement long. Ensuite je reconnais que la réalisation est intéressante, mais je trouve que ça se répète quoi la caméra qui bouge tout le temps.

Okay, the first thought I had as the movie was getting started was, holy shit the sound design and choreography in this movie is absolutely phenomenal. The first action scene is extremely memorable but the highlight is the sound and atmosphere throughout the entire movie. That’s the real star of the movie, sorry Tom Hanks. That’s where my praise ends for this movie. It’s a war movie but what war movies always get wrong is that patriotism/nationalism has no place in a war movie. It cheapens the horrors of war when this movie tries to have its cake and eat it too. It wants to say, “isn’t this horrible how so many people are needlessly dying?” But simultaneously makes it seem like the American troops are the heroes. I get that WWII is sort of a layup in that America was fighting true atrocities, but war movies love to gloss over the innocents from the opposition to instead focus on the militants from the “good side”. We see people kill enemies that have surrendered and disregard for civilians from Tom Hank’s troop. I think the only good war movie can be an anti-war movie which is not this movie. It glorifies war but wants to act like it shows how atrocious war is at the same time which makes it fail overall. But goddamn I love Tom Hanks and would be lying if the movie wasn’t solidly made and acted which earns it a three star rating despite my major flaws and concerns with the movie. It’s genuinely well made and had me invested the whole time, I just can’t get behind war.

too sentimental for realism, too realistic for sentimentalism Maybe my expectations were too high, maybe this film is mid, but regardless it was mostly a disappointment. The sound and visual design is outstanding, I can see how this movie was a major shift in the portrayal of combat and war on the screen. The story though… flat. This film felt more like an actual war experience, as in “I don’t know either why we’re here, it’s all sickening and horrible and tragic” and at the end, it goes nowhere. If there were guts to it, it would’ve went the All Quiet on the Western Front direction, but this way it just tried way too hard to do a “grim war story - big emotional impact” swing.

Is it a stretch of the imagination to say that Spielberg’s post Jurassic Park output paved the way to the modern American soft foot social liberal, moderate (whatever that means), and dimwitted patrio-fascist naval gazers falling comfortable beneath the Red, White, & Blue vail of American perspective as and all be all? Watching this today, does it not feel like a tailgate pregame for what is around the corner only 3 years later? To parade around how our good ol’ boys went to hell, lost their humanity, and sacrificed for the image of the modern nuclear family that mourns, but respects, the toll for the “moral” western world that couldn’t have been if American men didn’t lay down their lives— proliferating a white hot pride that feeds off a trauma permitting a people to believe in a blood spun twine, rather than collective history. Saving Private Ryan really does play as the perfect lab grown amalgamation of all of Spielberg’s idols, but without the kind of self awareness or conscious the likes of Fuller, Lean, or Kubrick had, it is the exact reason why he is the number one protégé of Ford. Because he cannot, no matter how socially liberal he was raised, get the poison out of his veins. He was possessed by crafts ability to be compelling, how fun action can be in the sense of dance and pulp slapping and apologizing to one another. When Spielberg took his formal elegance and sheen into the likes of The Color Purple or Empire of The Sun it didn’t play, it was only when he learned to embrace the European vérité in conjunction to the scale and painterly mosaics of Ford, that it cemented its tendrils into the minds of this nation. A little sick no? Probably Kamiński’s best.

Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan is a structurally interesting war film, and features several exceptional moments throughout but also some highly conventional war tropes and a weak plot which make the message of the film a little difficult to take at face value. Firstly, the film features one of the most iconic war sequences in film history, featuring flawless kinetic handheld cinematography and epic uses of quick zoom ins and camera movements, perfectly encapsulating the horrors of war. However, after that groundbreaking intro, I feel the film really loses its momentum rapidly. It evolves from a revolutionary war epic to a highly conventional and unoriginal war story, relying overly on traditional sentimentality (especially at the finale) and predictable war tropes. While the film throughout still continues to use groundbreaking techniques, it feels like a significant diminish in originality, making it feel quite generic overall, However despite its unoriginal plot, it still remains an highly impressive technical feat in cinematic history.

The opening D-day scene of Saving Private Ryan is rightly praised as being one of the greatest scenes in any war film. It is masterfully crafted by Spielberg and it makes you feel all the intesity and horror of war in your bones. The rest of the film, however, is not as fantastic. It doesn't seem to me that Spielberg is a serious enough person to be doing these historical dramas. Obviously I think that Schindlers list is somewhat of an exception to this but in this film he follows up his deveststing and intense opening with shmaultzy dramatics and ending it with just an action set piece. There are some great moments in here with one of Spielbergs bests scripts he has worked with that showcases some great character moments; however Spielberg was the wrong person to direct this tonally off-putting and overlong war film. definitely worth watching for many reasons and could maybe still be considered good but very messy.

I put this on during a flight from Europe thinking that I would watch the first half hour — a terrific and terrifically horrifying sequence of the Allied landing on Normandy — and then turn it off. But this time I was fascinated by the incredibly weird treatment of gender and watched it all the way through. The most striking scene in this respect is when the group of soldiers searching for Ryan are sitting in an abandoned church, lit only by candles, talking about their mothers. Borderline schmalzy and uncanny, this scene anticipates the *extremely* schmalzy closing scene, set decades in the future, when the now-aged Ryan tearfully asks his equally aged wife, “Am I a good man? Did I lead a good life?” Jeez guy please answer these questions for yourself. Women in this film exist only to be the passive foils of men, whether as bereaved mothers or supportive wives. The closest thing to an actual female character is a young French girl, maybe five years old, who is stranded in a bombed out building with her family. Her desperate father throws her down from above into the hands of one of the group of soldiers. After a fire fight, while the girl cowers among the soldiers, she is passed back to her father and the soldiers move on. The lesson here is that this world is an exclusively male one. Emotional complexity exists only among the men, whose relationships are at once fraternal, or father-son, or strangely erotic, with a tremendous sense of bodily intimacy. A very strange movie. Again, the terrible schmalzy ending is a huge misstep, much like the amazingly awkward ending of Schindler’s List. How you could make Jaws and then make those two is beyond me.

Look, I love me a good war story. Unfortunately, I have a soft spot for cute soldier guys or something like that I guess. But, this felt too much like propaganda, even for my liking. There was such a clear and egregious link between the Christian god, American ideals, and victory. Furthermore, it pushed a simplified concept of right and wrong/good and evil. Saving Private Ryan is in no way a bad movie. It just doesn’t consider the same things that I do going into a war film or war story. In war, everyone suffers. Soldiers are victims to the systems they trust and are brainwashed by. I want a complex look at this and all the moral dilemmas that go along with being on the battlefield. Other people just want a good American movie depicting our soldiers as brave heroes. And that’s fine, I suppose, just not what I’m looking for.
